items.title: Sid Ahmed Agoumi, monument du cinéma algérien, s’éteint à 86 ans
items.description: L’acteur et dramaturge Sid Ahmed Agoumi est décédé ce dimanche 20 septembre à 86 ans, a annoncé l’Office national des droits d'auteurs et droits voisins (ONDA). C’est un monument du cinéma algérien qui s’en va. De son vrai nom Sid Ahmed Meziane, le défunt est une figure emblématique du théâtre et du cinéma algériens. Sid Ahmed Agoumi, une carrière de plus de 60 ans Né en 1940 à Alger, Sid Ahmed Agoumi a un parcours artistique de plus de 60 ans, participant à des dizaines d'œuvres cinématographiques, télévisuelles et pièces de théâtre. Il a notamment joué dans « Z » de Costa-Gavras, l'unique œuvre algérienne oscarisée (1968), Les Hors-la-loi de Tewfik Farès (1969), Automne, octobre à Alger, de Mohamed Lakhdar Hamina (1993)… Installé en France depuis les années 1990, Agoumi a continué à apparaître dans des films de cinéma et de télévision. Il a aussi dirigé le Théâtre national algérien (TNA), les théâtres régionaux d’Annaba et de Constantine ainsi que la maison de la culture de Tizi-Ouzou. De nombreuses figures de l'art et de la culture ont tenu à lui rendre hommage dès l’annonce de son décès. Un homme « généreux, drôle, simple » L’ONDA a salué la mémoire d’une « figure emblématique du théâtre et du cinéma algériens ». « Avec son départ, la scène artistique algérienne perd une figure qui a laissé une empreinte indélébile dans le cœur de son public, ainsi qu’un parcours riche qui a fait de la scène et de l’écran des espaces de création et d’expression, et qui a contribué à enrichir le paysage culturel national par des rôles et des œuvres qui resteront gravés dans la mémoire de l’art algérien », a écrit le directeur de l'Office, Samir Thaalbi. « Sid Ahmed Agoumi nous quitte sur la pointe des pieds », a déploré pour sa part le réalisateur Bachir Derrais, qui dit avoir partagé avec le défunt « au moins un quart de siècle de travail, d’amitié, de complicité et surtout de fous rires ». « Une immense carrière, un parcours exemplaire, mais au-delà de l’acteur, je veux me souvenir de l’homme : généreux, drôle, simple », a ajouté le réalisateur à propos de celui qu'il a dirigé dans deux de ses films, Gourbi Palace (2006) et Llob (2009). « Adieu, Sid Ahmed Agoumi, artiste, homme et grand enfant innocent », a écrit de son côté le journaliste H’mida Ayachi sur sa page Facebook. L’article Sid Ahmed Agoumi, monument du cinéma algérien, s’éteint à 86 ans est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Once Home to Batman, This Faded Mansion Is Now Plagued by Real Bats
États-Unis : Trump interdit l’accès à la Maison Blanche à CNN, Politico et MS NOW
items.description: La confrontation entre Donald Trump et une partie de la presse americaine franchit une nouvelle etape. Le 19 septembre, des journalistes de CNN, Politico et MS NOW se sont vu refuser l'acces a la Maison Blanche. Leurs accreditations ont ete desactivees ou confisquees. Cette mesure fait suite a l'interdiction annoncee la veille par le president americain, qui accuse ces trois medias de diffuser de « fausses informations » sur son administration. La journaliste de CNN Betsy Klein a explique que des agents du Secret Service lui avaient indique que son badge avait ete desactive. Akayla Gardner, de MS NOW, et Cheyenne Haslett, de Politico, ont egalement ete empechees d'entrer. Les trois redactions ont annonce leur intention de defendre leur droit a couvrir la presidence americaine. Contraire au premier amendement Donald Trump a justifie sa decision en estimant que les medias ne devraient pas pouvoir publier ce qu'il qualifie de « fiction et de mensonges ». Il a egalement laisse entendre que d'autres titres pourraient etre concernes, citant notamment le New York Times et le Washington Post . La decision ouvre desormais une bataille juridique autour du premier amendement de la Constitution americaine, qui protege notamment la liberte de la presse. Plusieurs specialistes du droit cites par la presse americaine estiment qu'une administration ne peut exclure un media en raison du contenu de sa couverture des lors qu'elle accorde un acces a d'autres journalistes. La Maison Blanche avait deja ete confrontee a ce debat en 2018, apres le retrait de l'accreditation du journaliste de CNN Jim Acosta, finalement retablie a la suite d'une decision de justice. La White House Correspondents' Association a demande le retablissement immediat des accreditations, avertissant qu'un tel precedent pourrait permettre, a l'avenir, d'exclure n'importe quel media en fonction de sa couverture de l'actualite.

items.title: Interdiction du voile : après Ségolène Royal, Dominique de Villepin prend position
items.description: Dominique de Villepin, potentiel candidat à la présidentielle française, a pris clairement position sur le projet de Marine Le Pen d’interdire le port du voile islamique en France si elle accède à l’Élysée en 2027. « Je ne vois pas l'intérêt de détruire la paix sociale dans notre pays », a dénoncé l’ancien premier ministre de Jacques Chirac sur LCI samedi, en réponse aux propos de Marine le Pen sur le port du voile dans l’espace public. « Manifestement Marine Le Pen n’a pas la moindre idée de comment redresser le pays. Elle veut ouvrir un certain nombre de boîtes, comme l’immigration, la réforme de la Constitution, de façon à jouer les Français les uns contre les autres en stigmatisant. Et pour quel objectif ? C’est parce que quand on ne peut pas répondre aux problèmes des Français, on exclut » , a-t-il dit. Marine Le Pen veut interdire le port du voile en France Mardi, Marine Le Pen a confirmé son engagement d’interdire le port du voile dans l’espace public en France si elle est élue présidente de la République en 2027. « L'objectif sera d'interdire le voile et nous le ferons si les Français nous en donnent mandat « , a-t-elle dit. Ce projet divise profondément la France. L’extrême droite et la droite sont favorables alors que la gauche est opposée. Avant Dominique de Villepin, qui a jugé dangereux le projet de Marine le Pen, Ségolène Royal, candidate à la primaire socialiste du 9 octobre pour la prochaine présidentielle, a tranché la question. « Je ne ferai pas la chasse au foulard », a-t-elle déclaré. « Ce n’est pas la chasse au foulard qui va faire baisser le prix de l’essence ou éradiquer la pédocriminalité », a estimé la finaliste de la présidentielle de 2007. L’article Interdiction du voile : après Ségolène Royal, Dominique de Villepin prend position est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Constituency Games still a work in progress – Sports Minister
items.description: Ghana’s proposed Constituency Games remain a work in progress, according to Minister for Sports and Recreation Kofi Adams. “Constituency Games is still work in progress,” Mr Adams said in remarks shared by JoySports on SportsLink. The initiative is intended to create a structured pathway for young athletes to progress from community-level competition to regional and national championships. Under proposals previously outlined by National Paralympic Committee president Samson Deen, promising athletes could eventually be linked to scholarships, academies and national development programmes. The idea is to bring organised competition closer to communities while creating a clearer route for identifying and developing talent. Football, athletics, boxing and para-sports are among the disciplines proposed for the first edition of the Games. Mr Deen has also suggested that the programme could help identify athletes capable of representing Ghana at major international competitions, including the Olympic, Paralympic and World Championship levels. But questions around access, fairness and how athletes outside Accra will be included have also featured in consultations on the initiative. The proposed Games are not limited to athletes. Earlier plans have included opportunities to train young people in areas such as coaching, officiating and sports media, potentially creating wider skills and employment opportunities around community sport. For the programme to have a lasting impact, however, talent identification would need to be followed by regular coaching, competition and institutional support. Mr Adams also confirmed that the dissolved National Sports Authority board will soon be reconstituted, while leaving the door open for some former members to return. “We will soon reconstitute the new board. Some members of the dissolved board may still find themselves either on the same board or on other boards because they may still have some expertise to offer. “Some persons are also representing institutions, and those institutions may still have confidence in them to represent them. They may therefore be nominated again, so you may still find some of them on the new board,” he said. The Constituency Games are part of the wider sports development agenda under President John Dramani Mahama’s government, with the stated aim of strengthening grassroots participation and creating pathways for young talent. With Ghana preparing to mark its 70th independence anniversary in 2027, the Games could become an important part of efforts to strengthen community sport. For now, Mr Adams’s description of the initiative as “work in progress” means attention remains on when and how the plans will move from proposal to implementation.

items.title: Team Ghana set for historic Karting Africa Showrun in Angola
items.description: Ghana will make its first appearance on the international motorsport stage when a three-driver team competes at the Karting Africa Showrun in Angola next month. The team will travel to Benguela for the event, which takes place on 10 and 11 October 2026. The delegation, led by Auto Racing Ghana (ARG) president Samuel Moses Opoku-Agyemang, paid a courtesy call on National Sports Authority (NSA) Director-General Yaw Ampofo Ankrah in Accra. Senior driver Jihad Armand will be joined by junior drivers Khloé Kusi-Asomah, 11, and Ezra Stephens, 9. Armand has trained at the WORR Motorsport academy in South Africa, while the two junior drivers have been developing their interest in karting from an early age. The Karting Africa Showrun will bring together 39 drivers from across the continent and is expected to attract senior officials from the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA) and national motorsport authorities from across Africa. The event will also serve as a preview for the Karting Africa Cup, which is scheduled to run across five African countries in 2027. Mr Ampofo Ankrah said he was impressed by the team’s preparation despite limited resources and pledged the NSA’s support once Auto Racing Ghana completes its registration process. ARG says it is also working towards developing FIA-standard tracks in Ghana to support karting, road car clubs and driver development. The federation says the facilities could also support vehicle launches, test drives and science and engineering education. Its STEM Racing Ghana programme is targeting more than 100 schools and 10,000 students. ARG also plans to use motorsport to promote road safety, working with the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority, the Motor Traffic and Transport Department of the Ghana Police Service, the Ghana Standards Authority and the FIA. Ghana is scheduled to host the Karting Africa Showrun in 2027. Engineers & Planners is funding Team Ghana’s trip to Angola, with Imperial General Assurance, ASKY Airlines and Starbites also supporting the team.

items.title: Le Burkina et le Mali réaffirment leur solidarité à Niamey
items.description: Une délégation burkinabè et malienne, conduite par le général Célestin Simporé et comprenant notamment les ministres des Affaires étrangères des deux pays ainsi que le ministre malien de la Défense, a été reçue vendredi à Niamey par le président Abdourahamane Tiani, à la suite de la tentative de déstabilisation des 28 et 29 août. Le président Abdourahamane Tiani a reçu, vendredi 18 septembre 2026 au Palais de la Présidence à Niamey, une délégation du Burkina Faso et du Mali venue témoigner de la solidarité des deux pays après les événements survenus dans la nuit du 28 au 29 août, rapporte l’agence africaine de presse. La délégation était conduite par le général Célestin Simporé et comprenait notamment les ministres burkinabè et malien des Affaires étrangères, ainsi que le ministre malien de la Défense. « Au nom du peuple nigérien et en mon nom propre, je leur ai exprimé notre profonde gratitude. Cette visite est la preuve que l’AES est plus qu’une alliance, c’est une famille », a indiqué le général d’armée Abdourahamane Tiani dans un message publié au terme de l’audience. « L’ennemi ne dort pas, mais nous non plus. Nous resterons debout et unis », a ajouté le chef de l’État . Prenant la parole au terme de l’audience, le général Célestin Simporé a indiqué que la délégation avait été mandatée par le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, président du Burkina Faso, chef de l’État et président en exercice de la Confédération de l’AES. « La mission consiste à apporter le soutien des peuples du Burkina, des peuples du Mali, des présidents du Burkina Faso et des présidents du Mali aux autorités politiques du Niger et à l’ensemble des peuples nigériens », a-t-il déclaré dans un message relayé par le ministère burkinabè de la Défense. Selon le général Simporé, cette démarche vise à exprimer « une solidarité sans faille » au Niger et à soutenir la poursuite de la construction de la Confédération de l’AES. « Ceci nous rappelle toujours que l’AES doit se consolider davantage, arriver à des résultats probants parce que l’ennemi, comme vous le savez, ne dort pas », a-t-il poursuivi. Le général burkinabè a également présenté les condoléances des deux pays pour les pertes enregistrées lors des événements. « La tentative a occasionné des morts parmi les loyalistes. Donc nous prions que Dieu les accueille dans son paradis éternel », a-t-il déclaré. Au lendemain des événements, la Confédération des États du Sahel avait déjà réaffirmé son soutien aux autorités nigériennes. Dans un communiqué parvenu à APA, l’AES avait qualifié les faits d’« entreprise de déstabilisation » et indiqué que la tentative avait été contenue par les forces restées loyales aux institutions. L’organisation avait également salué la loyauté et le courage des Forces de défense et de sécurité nigériennes. L’article Le Burkina et le Mali réaffirment leur solidarité à Niamey est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Sénégal : Sadio Mané lance un projet agro-industriel de 11,7 milliards de FCFA
items.description: Suivant les pas de son aîné Seydou Keita du Mali qui a fait des investissements énormes au Mali, le sénégalais sadio Mane vient d’investir environ 12 milliards de francs CFA au Sénégal. L’international sénégalais Sadio Mané a procédé samedi à Bambali, dans la région de Sédhiou (sud), à la pose de la première pierre du projet SM10 Agro, un parc agro-industriel dédié à la production, au traitement et à la transformation de la mangue, pour un investissement estimé à près de 11,7 milliards de francs CFA, rapporte l’agence africaine de presse. La cérémonie, organisée à Kountoubou, village natal du footballeur, s’est déroulée en présence du ministre de l’Industrie et du Commerce, Serigne Guèye Diop, ainsi que des autorités administratives et territoriales et des acteurs du secteur agricole. Porté par SM10 Agro, filiale de SM10 Sénégal, le projet prévoit une station de traitement d’une capacité de 8 500 tonnes de mangues par an, trois unités de transformation pour la production de pulpe, de mangue séchée et de beurre de mangue, ainsi qu’une plantation progressive de 500 hectares de manguiers Kent. Le complexe comprendra également un centre de formation, un centre de recherche et développement, un système d’irrigation et des équipements de mécanisation agricole. Selon les promoteurs, le projet vise à réduire les pertes post-récolte, renforcer la transformation locale et développer des débouchés sur les marchés sénégalais, africains, européens et moyen-orientaux. « Aujourd’hui, nous semons » Prenant la parole lors de la cérémonie, Sadio Mané a rappelé son attachement à Bambali et sa volonté de contribuer au développement économique de son territoire d’origine. « Aujourd’hui, nous ne récoltons encore rien. Aujourd’hui, nous semons », a-t-il déclaré, en soulignant l’importance de créer des opportunités pour les jeunes et les femmes. Le projet prévoit à terme plus de 1 000 emplois directs et entend favoriser la formation et l’insertion des populations locales dans les métiers agricoles et agro-industriels. « Une réalité tangible » Le ministre de l’Industrie et du Commerce, Serigne Guèye Diop, a salué une initiative qui, selon lui, illustre la nécessité d’ancrer le développement industriel dans les territoires. « Le développement industriel de notre pays ne doit plus être un concept abstrait. Il doit être une réalité tangible, ancrée dans nos territoires », a-t-il déclaré. Il a également insisté sur la nécessité de transformer davantage les productions agricoles au Sénégal afin d’accroître la valeur créée localement. Le ministre a qualifié le projet de « pacte patriotique » et réaffirmé l’engagement de l’État à accompagner les investissements productifs contribuant à la transformation industrielle du pays. Le démarrage de la campagne industrielle de SM10 Agro est prévu à partir de mars 2027, après la finalisation des démarches techniques et administratives. À travers ce projet, Sadio Mané entend ainsi contribuer à faire de Bambali un pôle de production et de transformation de la mangue, au service du développement économique de la Casamance. Vivement que cet exemple soit suivi par d’autres célébrités africaines. items.title: Inondations à Coyah : La circulation est fortement perturbée ce dimanche
items.description: Au lendemain des fortes pluies qui ont touché la préfecture de Coyah dans la nuit du vendredi 18 au samedi 19 septembre 2026, la circulation reste fortement perturbée dans certains endroits. De la mosquée de Somayah jusqu’au pont de Sambaya, la situation est particulièrement difficile. L’ancien pont ayant cédé sous la pression des eaux, un important embouteillage s’est formé, rendant la circulation très difficile pour les usagers. Selon Aboubacar Camara, la circulation est devenue particulièrement dense depuis la rupture de l’ancien pont. Même constat pour Alseny Sylla, qui appelle à la mise en place de mesures d’urgence afin de rétablir rapidement la circulation. Au moment de notre départ des lieux, les usagers étaient toujours confrontés à d’importants embouteillages sur cet axe.

items.title: TTAP forms committee to consult with political parties, reach consensus on multi-party moot
items.description: Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) on Sunday formed a six-member committee to hold consultations with political parties and reach an agreement on the agenda for a proposed multi-party conference (MPC). The opposition had announced the proposed moot earlier this month. In a post on social media platform X, the opposition alliance announced the formation of the six-member committee, which will include: Leader of the Opposition in the Senate Allama Raja Nasir Abbas; PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan; TTAP’s Secretary General Asad Qaiser; Vice Chairman Mustafa Nawaz Khokhar; spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmed Yousafzai; and PTI core committee member Khalid Yousaf Chaudhry. According to the statement, the committee will liaise with other political parties regarding the proposed moot, consult them on its agenda and work towards reaching agreement on the way forward. The notification said the committee would continue its consultation and coordination process under the guidance of the TTAP leadership. On Sept 11, the opposition announced it intended to hold consultations to call an MPC to discuss several issues, including the creation of new provinces, law and order and the economy. At the time, Barrister Gohar, speaking to the media after a meeting of his party with Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam–Fazl (JUI-F), had outlined plans to hold the conference, saying that “the current law and order situation, the economy, inflation, lawlessness, and the creation of new provinces issue” called for such measures.

items.title: 52-year-old South African arrested with suspected heroin after arriving from Accra
items.description: A 52-year-old South African man has been arrested at OR Tambo International Airport after police allegedly found suspected heroin worth more than R2 million, equivalent to a little over 1.4 million Ghana cedis, in his luggage. The arrest was made on Sunday, September 20, during an intelligence-led operation conducted by the South African Police Service (SAPS), with support from the Border Management Authority (BMA). According to SAPS, the suspect had just arrived on a flight from Accra, Ghana, when he was intercepted at the airport. A search of his luggage allegedly uncovered bullet-shaped objects and blocks containing substances suspected to be heroin. The drugs have an estimated street value of more than R2 million. The latest arrest brings to three the number of suspected drug mules arrested at OR Tambo International Airport in the past three weeks as authorities intensify operations against drug trafficking. Suspect to face drug trafficking charges The suspect is expected to appear before the Kempton Park Magistrates’ Court later this week, where he is expected to face drug trafficking-related charges. Read Also: Mahama directs inter-agency task force to submit roadmap to deal with drug trafficking in two weeks SAPS said investigations are continuing to establish the source of the suspected drugs and determine whether the suspect was linked to a wider trafficking network. The police have pledged to continue intelligence-led and targeted operations aimed at disrupting drug trafficking syndicates. Read Also: French customs seize cocaine worth $260m inside shipment from Ghana This comes after several incidents of reported drug shipments from Ghana, which have forced the presidency to commission a task force to investigate those cases following the arrests of some suspects .

items.title: Promotions immobilières à Alger : l’irréparable évité de justesse à Tixeraine
items.description: « Nous nous demandons qui donne ces autorisations, où sont les autorités… ». L’homme qui parle ainsi est un citoyen excédé par ce qu'il est advenu du quartier de Tixeraine, Alger, par la faute de la prolifération anarchique des promotions immobilières privées . Dans une vidéo diffusée sur les réseaux sociaux, il partage des images choquantes en effet. On y voit des bâtiments de plus de dix étages en construction, collés les uns aux autres, sans espace vert ni respect des règles de l’urbanisme moderne. « Construire tout cela sur un espace de 500 mètres carrés, où va-t-on comme ça ? », se demande-t-il. L’homme a décidé d'exprimer son ras-le-bol après qu’un de ces chantiers a causé un glissement qui a entraîné l'effondrement de la chaussée. Un drame a été évité de justesse. Ce cas n’est malheureusement pas isolé. À El Biar, le promoteur immobilier Ahmed Toubal a effectué des travaux de terrassement pour transformer une maison en un immeuble de plusieurs étages, et a mis en danger l’habitation mitoyenne. Malgré les réclamations des riverains, la mairie d’El Biar n’a pas réagi. Le chantier fonctionne de jour et de nuit, avec des travailleurs égyptiens et subsahariens qui passent parfois la nuit sur place dans des conditions lamentables. À Alger, les promotions immobilières continuent de pousser comme des champignons. Entre nuisances des chantiers, mise en danger des constructions mitoyennes et défiguration de l’aspect des villes, les griefs ne manquent pas à l'égard de ces ensembles d'habitations censés être des cadres de vie agréables, mais où la quantité et le gain ont, hélas, pris le pas sur la qualité. Résidences huppées ou cités-dortoirs ? Certains quartiers de la capitale sont particulièrement privilégiés par les promoteurs pour des raisons antagonistes : soit parce que le foncier est accessible, soit, au contraire, il est très rare et cher, ce qui permet de vendre les futurs appartements à des prix excessifs. À Tixeraine, jadis petit quartier de la commune de Birkhadem aux maisons clairsemées, les « promotions » sortent de terre à un rythme effréné. Les terrains nus étant rares dans les quartiers mitoyens de Saïd Hamdine, de Bir Mourad Rais et de Hydra, c’est sur Tixeraine que se ruent les promoteurs. Depuis quelques années, les nouveaux bâtiments contrastent avec les petites bâtisses du vieux village. Et ça continue de pousser. Même si les appartements se négocient au prix fort, les nouvelles constructions dans plusieurs quartiers de la capitale sont plus proches de la cité dortoir surpeuplée que de la résidence huppée, calme et commode. Appât du gain… La raison est que pour faire un maximum de gain, les promoteurs font un maximum d'étages. Et le même appât du gain fait naître de nouveaux projets à proximité. L’expansion est à la fois verticale et horizontale. Parfois, les fenêtres et les balcons se font face à quelques mètres d’espace et les rues deviennent trop exiguës pour contenir le trafic. Les espaces verts sont souvent inexistants, le foncier étant trop cher pour sacrifier le moindre mètre carré. Sur les réseaux sociaux, les habitants, excédés par ce qu'ils constatent, partagent sur les réseaux sociaux des vidéos qui attestent du massacre. C’est le cas notamment à Bordj El Kiffan. Dans cette commune de la côte Est de la capitale, c’est le foncier pas trop cher qui attire. Les images partagées sont hallucinantes, avec des immeubles collés les uns aux autres, des ruelles exiguës. Il est incompréhensible que des autorisations soient accordées pour de telles constructions qui font fi des moindres règles de l’urbanisme. Une passivité qui interpelle Dans bien des cas, la réglementation n’est pas plus respectée pendant les travaux de réalisation. Certains chantiers travaillent même la nuit pour livrer les appartements dans les délais, causant des nuisances insupportables aux riverains. Parfois, ce sont des bâtiments ou villas qui sont mis en danger par les travaux d'excavation, quand ce ne sont pas les réseaux souterrains d'énergie ou d'évacuation qui sont endommagés. Beaucoup se demandent ce qu'il adviendra à ce rythme des villes algériennes – car le phénomène ne se limite pas à Alger. Les citoyens et les associations se plaignent et tirent la sonnette d'alarme sur les réseaux sociaux et se demandent pourquoi tant de passivité. L’article Promotions immobilières à Alger : l’irréparable évité de justesse à Tixeraine est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Carburants en France : Le prix du gazole franchit la barre record de 2,41 euros le litre
items.description: Le prix du gazole en France a atteint 2,41 euros en moyenne, dimanche, un nouveau record en pleine crise géopolitique où les approvisionnements sont fortement perturbés. Dans le détail, le prix du litre de gazole atteint 2,4097 euros, selon une moyenne calculée par les analystes et rapportée par les médias français à partir des prix affichés dimanche pour plus de 8.700 stations-service, dépassant ainsi le record établi la veille. Le SP95-E10, carburant le plus vendu en France, évolue depuis plus d'une dizaine de jours au-dessus de son pic de 2022, relève la même source, ajoutant que le SP98 dépasse, quant à lui, 2,28 euros en moyenne, selon une moyenne enregistrée dans plus de 6.800 stations. La flambée des prix du carburant depuis fin février provoquée par la guerre en Iran alimente une tension sociale déjà matérialisée jeudi par des blocages de dépôt pétroliers par des pêcheurs en Méditerranée. Toutes les stations n'actualisent pas quotidiennement leurs tarifs. Pour le calcul de la moyenne, l’analyse a été basée sur les stations ayant renseigné un prix sur le site gouvernemental il y a moins de 31 jours. Ce délai est rallongé quand le prix paraît volontairement plafonné, comme cela est pratiqué par les stations TotalEnergies, indique-t-on. items.title: Colloque à Tunis | Les causes de l’infertilité et les moyens d’y remédier
items.description: Les difficultés à procréer sont un phénomène croissant au sein de la société tunisienne, a indiqué le président de la Société tunisienne de gynécologie-obstétrique (STGO) et chef du service de gynécologie-obstétrique de Bizerte, Mechaal Mourali, lors des travaux des 5 èmes Journées de la médecine reproductive, consacrées au traitement de l’infertilité et au recul de l’âge de la procréation, qui se tiennent les 19 et 20 septembre 2026 à Gammarth, au nord de Tunis, sous l’égide de la STGO. Dr Mourali attribue cette évolution à plusieurs facteurs, notamment la pollution et le mode de vie, ainsi que le stress, la sédentarité, l’obésité, le tabagisme et la consommation d’alcool et de drogues. Ces facteurs peuvent affecter la fertilité tant chez l’homme que chez la femme — en altérant la qualité des spermatozoïdes ou des ovocytes — et ainsi accroître les difficultés de procréation, a souligné le praticien, en expliquant que l’amélioration de la fertilité ne dépend pas uniquement des techniques médicales modernes, mais commence également par une modification du mode de vie — notamment la pratique d’une activité physique, la réduction du stress et l’arrêt du tabac — autant de facteurs susceptibles d’accroître les chances de conception. Les progrès des techniques de procréation assistée ont également contribué à améliorer les taux de réussite, a aussi indiqué Dr Mourali, tout en évoquant le rôle que peut jouer l’intelligence artificielle pour aider les médecins et les couples à choisir les meilleures options thérapeutiques, y compris pour l’évaluation et la sélection des spermatozoïdes et des ovocytes les plus appropriés. Le colloque a également abordé le rôle de la chirurgie dans le traitement de certaines causes de difficultés de procréation. Certaines interventions chirurgicales peuvent en effet contribuer à améliorer la fertilité et à traiter divers problèmes rencontrés par les femmes. Dr Mourali a insisté sur le fait que la combinaison de changements de mode de vie, de techniques modernes et, si nécessaire, de la chirurgie, offre de multiples options thérapeutiques pour faire face aux difficultés de procréation. items.title: Shatta Wale challenges UPSA students to build entrepreneurial mindsets
items.description: Ghanaian musician and entrepreneur Charles Nii Armah Mensah Jr., popularly known as Shatta Wale, has challenged students of the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA) to cultivate entrepreneurial mindsets to ensure their success. The award-winning artiste urged young people to look beyond academic qualifications and focus on developing the mindset needed to identify and seize opportunities in an increasingly competitive world. Shatta Wale said this while addressing students at the UPSA 1000 and Ghana Entrepreneurship Conference. The event formed part of the University’s entrepreneurship and mentorship initiative aimed at exposing students to practical industry experiences, leadership insights and entrepreneurial opportunities. The programme brings together accomplished professionals, business executives and innovators to inspire students and prepare them for the world of work and enterprise development. “The deepest part of my journey isn’t the song, it isn’t the crowd, it isn’t even one particular business. It is the mind that keeps evolving,” Shatta Wale said. He encouraged students not to imitate his lifestyle or public persona but rather learn from his way of thinking, adaptability and determination. “Don’t copy my life. What I would rather let you copy is my thinking,” he stated, stressing that personal growth and success were rooted in discipline, self-belief and lifelong learning. The musician, who has built a career spanning music production, digital content distribution, and entrepreneurship, shared insights into how he leveraged technology and online platforms to generate income and expand his brand beyond entertainment. He noted that many young people were yet to fully appreciate the opportunities available through technology and the digital economy. “Success begins with vision and preparation. You have to see it before everybody sees it and believe it before everybody believes it. When you don’t see yourself as the next chartered accountant or the next billionaire, nobody will see it for you,” he added. The artiste urged the students to transform challenges into opportunities by developing problem-solving skills, investing wisely and continuously upgrading their knowledge. He advised them to turn “problems into questions, questions into ideas, ideas into actions, income into assets and success into another opportunity.” Shatta Wale cautioned against complacency, saying that achieving financial success should not mark the end of personal ambition and growth. “Don’t let success make your mind lazy. Keep learning, keep asking, keep building and keep evolving because a powerful mind is not a mind that knows everything; it is a mind that refuses to stop learning,” he said. He emphasised that before building wealth or businesses, young people must first develop the capacity to manage and sustain them. “Before you build the money, build the mind that can manage the money. Before you build the business, build the mind that can lead the business. Before you build the empire, build the mind that won’t destroy the empire,” he advised. Born Charles Nii Armah Mensah Jr., Shatta Wale is one of Ghana’s most influential music personalities and entrepreneurs. Over the years, he has built a strong brand in the entertainment industry while expanding into business ventures and digital enterprises, earning recognition for his resilience, reinvention and entrepreneurial approach to career development.

items.title: Burkina/ Hakili Mousso 2026 : L'excellence scientifique féminine à l'honneur
items.description: Le Premier ministre Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo a présidé, le samedi 19 septembre 2026 à Ouagadougou, la cérémonie de distinction des lauréates de la première édition du concours national Hakili Mousso. L'information est rapportée par la Primature du Burkina Faso. Cette initiative vise à promouvoir l'excellence scientifique féminine et à encourager les jeunes filles à s'engager dans les disciplines scientifiques. Ouvert aux bachelières de la session 2026, le concours a porté sur les mathématiques, la physique et la chimie. En chimie, Inès Nikiema a remporté le premier prix avec 18,73/20, tandis qu'Aminata Traoré s'est classée première en physique avec 15/20. En mathématiques, Adjaratou Bama a obtenu la première place avec 14,25/20. C'est après les sélections régionales que 84 candidates ont pris part à la finale nationale, à l'issue de laquelle cinq prix ont été attribués dans chacune des trois disciplines, avec notamment des récompenses financières, des motos, des ordinateurs, des bourses et des bons de carburant. La cérémonie a également mis en lumière la sous-représentation des filles dans les filières scientifiques. Selon les données présentées, elles représentaient 36,7% des effectifs des filières scientifiques en 2025-2026, contre 59,5% dans les filières non scientifiques. Le concours est ainsi présenté comme un moyen d'encourager davantage de jeunes filles à s'orienter vers les sciences, les technologies et les domaines industriels. Le Premier ministre a également souligné le rôle des enseignants et des parents dans l'accompagnement des jeunes filles et a appelé les lauréates à poursuivre leur engagement dans les domaines scientifiques. Les lauréates ont pour leur part, pris l'engagement de devenir des ambassadrices de la science et de mettre leurs compétences au service du Burkina Faso. Lefaso.net Source : Primature du Burkina Faso

items.title: The Pinball President
items.description: In 1946, the year that Donald Trump was born, the pinball machine offered everything but control. The bumpers were propulsive, the lights flashed, but the player’s only honest move was to pull a spring-loaded plunger. After that, the ball belonged to the machine, zinging and zooming wherever the bumpers sent it. This is how many Americans experience the Trump presidency today: antic caroming that they can do little more than watch. The ballroom. The Iran war. The threats against Canada. Greenland. Portraits of himself as Christ, a decorated general, or the pope. The arch. The Kennedy Center. Prosecution of enemies. Pardons. Imaginary Reflecting Pool vandals. Federal incursions into voting. Tariffs on. Tariffs off. Tariffs on again. The Qatari plane. Endless promises—to release tax returns, to end corruption, to deliver $5,000 checks—that never materialize. No president has been more with us than Trump, because no president has been better at seizing public attention. But there is a difference between getting attention and doing something with it. For months, the president has been unable to convince the public that he’s up to the job. In a CNN poll released at the end of July, 65 percent of respondents said that his policies had worsened the economy, and only 28 percent approved of his handling of Iran. Voters have watched the caroming and have concluded that he doesn’t have his eye on the ball. They care about the economy, and he seems to care about everything else. Only 27 percent of adults told CNN that Trump has the right priorities, down from 45 percent when the term began. And a record 73 percent said he hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important issues. In June, while Trump was fixated on the Reflecting Pool and stopping widespread voter fraud that doesn’t exist, a bipartisan housing bill aimed at high costs reached his desk. He called it “a big yawn” and said he hadn’t decided whether to sign it. In July, he let it become law without his signature. This is a problem for Republicans in November 2026, but it’s an opportunity for voters looking to November 2028. Once a roster of candidates emerges, their supporters will discover that the office demands—wouldn’t you know it?—exactly the qualities that their preferred candidate happens to possess. Now, when there’s no one horse to back, is the time to use the current president’s rat-a-tat treatment of our attention to ask how we want the next president to spend it. Many voters will ask only one thing of the next president: Don’t be Donald Trump . Fair enough. But stopping at “not Trump” wastes the extremity of the Trump years. Extremes clarify. A flood shows you where the ground was always low. The Trump years have been a reminder that the presidency is a trust. The public’s attention belongs to the public. A president borrows it, and the test at every turn is whether he spends it on their account or his own. Trump treats it as a possession, to do with as he pleases, like the East Wing. For him, the public is his cheering section. A president who ignores the half of the country that voted against him teaches them that elections are conquests. They will remember that when they win. [ Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer: ‘I run the country and the world’ ] It’s true that when Trump wants to focus the nation’s attention on something, he is relentless: immigration, his enemies, his ballroom. In April, The Washington Post found that he had publicly mentioned the ballroom on roughly a third of the days by that point in the year; he had posted about it more than about tariffs. But what he cares about often isn’t in the nation’s greater interest. A trustee doesn’t spend the trust on himself. The next president should ration his calls on the public’s attention, which, after all, protects his own effectiveness and the country’s. “Public psychology,” Franklin Roosevelt wrote in 1935 to a reporter urging him to speak out more often, “cannot, because of human weakness, be attuned for long periods of time to a constant repetition of the highest note in the scale.” When Roosevelt did speak, he explained. In his first fireside chat, he walked the country through how a bank works. Explanation is what lets a president speak less: A public that has been shown why can carry the argument on its own, and a public that has only been told what must be told again tomorrow. A president cannot push opinion where it doesn’t want to go, only nudge it, and that is possible only if he hasn’t already worn the audience out. A president who is always talking cannot use talking to signal that this time matters . The creed of this current era is the opposite. “If you’re not making news, you’re not governing,” wrote former Representative Matt Gaetz, who made news nearly every day he served and governed not at all. A president who consumes the country’s attention spends down a resource that citizens need for their own affairs, including those delightful corners of human experience that should be free of political consideration. The UFC fighter Bryce Mitchell understood this before the bouts on the White House lawn this summer. Mitchell, who did not participate, said that the government was “desecrating its role in society.” The government, he said, “is supposed to protect us, not entertain us.” Sometimes a president doesn’t have to ask for the country’s attention, because catastrophe has already gathered it. In these cases, a president can act as a moral force, particularly in consolation. Reagan after the Challenger explosion, Clinton after the Oklahoma City bombing, the younger Bush after the attacks of 9/11, and Obama at Emanuel AME in Charleston, South Carolina. Each president spent the nation’s attention on its grief and, in doing so, reminded the nation what it valued. Trump has nearly erased this part of the job, inventing a new one in its place: chief grave dancer. When Rob Reiner was murdered in December, Trump blamed Reiner himself; when Robert Mueller died in March, Trump wrote , “Good, I’m glad he’s dead.” A president sends a moral signal not just in the words he uses but also in what he chooses to spend them on. After the white-nationalist march and the death of Heather Heyer in Charlottesville, Virginia, in August 2017, Trump denounced the Nazis, but the thrust of his attention was aimed elsewhere. He obsessed over the counterprotesters. He praised himself for being the only one brave enough to name what he claimed were the misdeeds of the people opposing the Nazis. “You had a group on one side that was bad, and you had a group on the other side that was also very violent,” he insisted without evidence, “and nobody wants to say it, but I will say it right now.” He sent six tweets about Charlottesville and, in those tweets, never used the terms racism , bigotry , or white nationalism . He sent 37 tweets about NFL players kneeling during the anthem. All of this happens where we can see it. We tend to treat the presidency as if it existed only in that public form. Most of it doesn’t. Because much of the job happens in secret or out of camera range, what the president chooses to do with public attention is our best evidence of how he sorts the world in private. That evidence has limits. A president who never mentions the deficit might be working on it every morning. Eisenhower’s style was called the “hidden hand”: The president who looked idle at the podium was working the levers out of sight. But a president whose public attention shows no discipline, discernment, or patience isn’t going to discover those attributes at the necessary scale when the cameras turn away. Trump governs by the Heisman hand, always in your face. [ George T. Conway III: Unfit for office ] The presidency demands brutal prioritization. “I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important,” goes a line that Eisenhower liked to quote . “The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.” It was such a simple idea that it became the Eisenhower Matrix, used by managers everywhere to sort incoming challenges. The principle applies with more force in a job where the urgent arrives by the hour. If missile stockpiles are low, we want a president fixing that now, not giving a speech about the deficit. But we also want a president who can see the deficit coming and feel some obligation to the future citizens who will live under galactic debt. Trump spends a lot of his time on matters that are neither important nor urgent. The New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman, who has covered Trump for 30 years, has said that if you charted his mind these days, 70 percent of it would go to gilding, construction, renaming, and tribute projects. The exhaustion after Trump will produce an appetite for quiet. It has happened before. George W. Bush campaigned on restoring dignity to the office because Americans were worn out by the dramas of the Clinton years; he wanted a presidency that his team promised would show up on page A24 of the newspaper. But quiet is not a standard. The office needs a benchmark built from the job itself, not from the last man to hold it. Nor should the next president react to Trump’s frivolity by turning every subject into a family talk in the living room about Important Matters—a brittle standard where partisans adopt the posture of the online scold who answers “I love dogs” with “Your silence on cats is deafening.” Under that standard, a president must speak to everything, and a president who speaks to everything has no time left to do anything. Campaigns often measure for qualities that have little or nothing to do with the office. But voters can evaluate how candidates treat public attention on the campaign trail and make some inferences about how they would approach the job. Here are some questions to ask: Does the candidate choose problems that a president can actually move, and can he say why those and not others? Can a president articulate a vision for the country to people who are not likely to vote for her? Can he explain rather than merely assert? Does she ever talk about a problem that won’t pay off before the next election? Can he let a news cycle pass without joining it? And when grief or outrage arrives, does he show any evidence of a concern for the entire nation? How a candidate handles these moments during a campaign—when public attention, ever more scarce in the age of the algorithm, is the only thing he has to spend—tells us how that candidate will spend ours. In 1947, the year after Trump’s birth, pinball changed. The flipper was added, which meant the player was no longer merely watching. Where the ball went was now, at least in part, up to the player. In 2028, voters will be in the game again. But that requires attention to the office now.

items.title: A Show That Lovingly Pokes Fun at Gen Z
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Emma Williams, an associate editor who helps oversee the magazine’s social media and has also written about her home state of Texas . Emma is a habitual rewatcher of Normal People , a show that she says has resonated with her differently over time. She also enjoys listening to her namesake Emmylou Harris, laughing over Adults episodes, and watching Hailee Catalano’s comforting cooking videos. — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor The television show I’m most enjoying right now: The first scene of FX’s Adults tells you pretty much everything you need to know about the show: It’s crass, crude, absurd, and indulgently hilarious . Adults pokes fun at Gen Z without being judgmental or predictable, and it features some familiarly ridiculous plights. Maybe don’t watch it with your grandmother—but your spunky aunt is probably okay. A quiet song that I love: I discovered the British DJ Fred Again when I was going down an NPR Tiny Desk Concert rabbit hole years ago. I was immediately struck by his talent—but over time, I have come to better appreciate the emotion he evokes through his performances. Even in his natural habitat, behind the DJ booth, Fred isn’t what you might normally expect from an EDM artist: He samples spoken-word poems, Zoom calls, and random internet videos to create songs that you can just as easily dance to as you can cry to. I know I’m cheating a bit by saying that his entire Tiny Desk production is my favorite quiet song, but the fact that he was able to pull off an acoustic EDM performance is remarkable. To re-create the sound of electronic beats, he used the marimba, the vibraphone, and the piano; he also pounded and tapped on a desk and layered in his soft, husky voice. It is gentle, engrossing, and stupidly impressive. A loud song that I love: The first time I heard “Dance Yrself Clean,” by LCD Soundsystem, I was confused. My best friend played it for me, and by minute two, I was enjoying the song, but I could not comprehend how this hazy and somewhat repetitive tune could continue for another seven minutes and be as “life changing” as she had promised. Then I hit 3:05 on the track. I felt the ba-da-da-dum in my bones before James Murphy’s newly impassioned voice flooded through the speakers. This is now my song for any moment when I need to drown out my thoughts. Whether I’m going through a breakup, a bad day, or an existential crisis, I’ll put on “Dance Yrself Clean” and itch through the first three minutes, eagerly anticipating the rush of euphoria that hits after the beat drops. Years later, that same friend and I heard the song live. I have no idea whether we were crying or laughing or shouting, but I know we were dancing with abandon—and letting the music wash over us. A cultural product I loved as a teenager and still love: I watched Normal People for the first time when I was 19, and I’ve rewatched it at least once a year every year since. I have never wavered in my fondness for it, but my reaction to the characters and storylines has evolved with time. When I first saw the show, based on Sally Rooney’s novel of the same name, I fell madly in love with Connell, barely registering that his cold avoidance of Marianne in public was wrong. I just thought he was broody and complicated; therefore, to my teenage mind, he was perfect and dreamy. I’m glad to say that I have moved past that (kind of), and I now find it difficult to watch his treatment of Marianne in the first few episodes. In my 20s, I resonate more with Marianne’s college arc. Specifically, her need to become the coolest, most stylish, most successful version of herself—even if it comes at the cost of her own happiness. Marianne and Connell’s lack of clear communication is always maddening. But I understand it more with age. Sometimes vocalizing what you really want can be more terrifying than staying quiet. A musical artist who means a lot to me: I have to pay homage to my namesake, the inimitable country folk artist Emmylou Harris. Her music reminds me of my home state of Texas. Listening to her song “Boulder to Birmingham” transports me back to long drives through the plains of West Texas and the seemingly endless miles of wind turbines. I hear my parents’ voices, lovingly calling me Emmylou and Emmy-lou-lou. Whenever I feel adrift, her music pulls me back to the ground. A YouTuber, TikToker, Twitch streamer, or other online creator I’m a fan of: I have an embarrassing confession: There is a cooking influencer whom I’m really obsessed with—as in, I went to a meet and greet of hers, and I send her the occasional tipsy Instagram DM. (Sometimes she even responds!) Hailee Catalano is a James Beard–winning chef. Her food is fresh and unique, and her video style isn’t gimmicky or aggressive like that of so many other cooking accounts—it’s simple and personable. My favorite series of hers is called Friday Night Dinner , which is a collaboration with her partner, Chuck Cruz, who is also a chef and content creator. They film themselves making a new meal every week, and I can only describe their vibe as homey. The videos sometimes have awkward pauses and funny asides (and, of course, clips of their dog, Gus), and watching them makes me feel like I’m sitting at the kitchen counter as two of my friends prepare something delicious for us to eat. A poem, or line of poetry, that I return to: The older I get, the more I find myself recalling the lines of Langston Hughes’s poem “ Harlem .” Hughes asks: “What happens to a dream deferred?” I recently turned 25, and the “quarter-life crisis” is certainly hitting me. I think about all of my childhood hopes that have dissipated, and all of the ones I still have that I’m not sure will come true. I, too, wonder what happens to these dreams. Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic : George Packer on sons and mothers Anne Applebaum: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption. What comes after America The Week Ahead Primetime , a crime thriller about the rise of the To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen and the world of televised vigilantism (in theaters Friday) Youth , a comedic-drama series about a 50-year-old divorcée balancing dating with caring for her aging parents and adult son (streaming today on HBO Max) Mazywood , a horror novel by Tananarive Due about a man uncovering the truth about his grandmother, set in Old Hollywood and the present day (out Tuesday) Essay Illustration by Alisa Gao / The Atlantic Math Can’t Go On Like This By Kai Williams In late July, one of the world’s most famous mathematicians issued a warning to his field. Math is entering a “turbulent period,” the UCLA professor Terence Tao said in front of a packed lecture hall at the International Congress of Mathematicians. AI is getting so good at math, he said, that it’s causing a “crisis in our mathematical values and practices.” Earlier in the same week that Tao gave his talk at math’s most prestigious conference, a researcher at Anthropic had used Claude to disprove an 87-year-old math conjecture. Still, when I asked mathematicians at the conference about their experiences with AI, most hadn’t thought deeply about the topic. Many seemed a little surprised that a journalist was asking them about it at all. Read the full article. More in Culture An ingredient that’s all too rare in adult life A shouting match and an ultimatum at the Kennedy Center The next change Trump has planned for the Smithsonian A night for actor’s actors, not movie stars The knives are out for Bill Belichick. Catch Up on The Atlantic What Trump’s bizarre posts are teaching us about AI Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is enormous. Ian Bogost: College is coming apart. Photo Album Willem de Kooning, Excavation , 1950. (The Willem de Kooning Foundation / Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York. Photo by Robert Lifson.) Willem de Kooning took the language of drawing, ripped it up, and rearranged it, Sebastian Smee writes. Take a look at some of his drawings from a new exhibition about the influential abstract expressionist—and read about what he had to unlearn. Rafaela Jinich contributed to this newsletter. Play our daily crossword. Explore all of our newsletters. When you buy a book using a link in this newsletter, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic .

items.title: Guatemala’s Democracy Dilemma
items.description: J ust over three years ago in Guatemala, a coalition of young and Indigenous voters helped propel Bernardo Arévalo, a reformer who campaigned against corruption, to an astounding presidential win. Guatemala had not only refused the global trend toward populist authoritarianism; it had also defied what its citizens called “the pact of the corrupt,” a loose alliance of politicians, judges, criminal networks, and crony capitalists that had gained control of the country’s institutions. Today the mood in Guatemala is less hopeful. Some of Arévalo’s former allies, and many of those who voted for him, are dejected, convinced that the president missed a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform the country. When I met with Arévalo in Guatemala City in May, he defended the pace of his administration’s progress and suggested that the alternative would have been to abuse the powers of a government he was elected to reform. In Latin America, “we never truly got used to understanding that the rule of law is fundamental,” he told me. “Rule of law is not the same as rule by law. Rule of law is when we all accept that we are subject to the law and we operate within that framework to solve problems. Rule by law is when I use the law that’s at my disposal as part of my political arsenal.” Had he crossed that line, Arévalo insisted, he would have risked being ousted by his opponents and replaced by someone willing to do much worse. His critics disagree. Arévalo’s personal integrity is undisputed. But some of the reformers who helped elect him now argue that he may be too scrupulously rules-respecting to deal effectively with the “pact of the corrupt” and the institutions it captured—too much of a liberal democrat to save democracy. When he leaves office in 2028, they fear that the pact will quickly retake control of the few institutions it has lost, or that voters will choose an autocrat who promises to crush crime without concern for legality. Guatemala’s predicament points to a more universal problem. Can liberal reformers unwind authoritarian state capture without, themselves, engaging in at least a little bit of illiberalism? The dilemma is not Guatemala’s alone. Move too aggressively, and you risk being branded an autocrat, or even becoming one. Move too cautiously, and you risk obstruction, sabotage, and ineffectuality. South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa chose a gradualist approach to reversing Jacob Zuma’s state capture and disappointed many of his supporters. Placing the opposite bet, Poland’s Donald Tusk bent rules to try to undo the damage done by the right-populist Law and Justice party—and stood accused of undermining the rule of law. Hungary’s post-Orbán leader, Péter Magyar, seems to be following Tusk’s example. [ Read: How to defeat a mafia state ] In a way, both Arévalo and his critics are right. Guatemala has avoided a democratic breakdown. But the president’s rules-bound approach has also left many Guatemalans feeling that he has not fought for them forcefully enough. The question now is whether Arévalo has preserved democracy as an ideal that Guatemalans believe in and, if necessary, will defend. I n Guatemala City , I watched as hundreds of people gathered outside the country’s public prosecutor’s office, a bunker-like building ringed by a huge black-steel fence put up three years before, allegedly to shield the occupants from nonviolent democracy protesters. The crowd had come to celebrate the long-awaited end to the term of María Consuelo Porras, the country’s attorney general and, to many citizens, the personification of the pact of the corrupt. For the past eight years, Porras had been a figure of fear. She used the power of her position to investigate and jail critics of state corruption. When Arévalo was elected in 2023, her office tried to overturn the results, alleging irregularities that international observers found baseless. That effort looked likely to succeed—until indigenous Maya communities organized peaceful demonstrations that lasted 106 days and drew the participation of nearly 2 million Guatemalans. Arévalo was inaugurated. That he did not take extralegal action to remove Porras from her post has given rise to some of the fiercest criticism against him. She opened an investigation into Arévalo’s party, the Seed Movement, for relatively minor party-registration irregularities. Although the probe did not produce formal charges, it led to the party’s dissolution and thus thwarted any hope of its controlling Congress. Porras also brought more than 75 legal cases or complaints against the president and his supporters, including the arrests of two of the Indigenous leaders behind the 2023 protests, and even a cabinet minister. Now Porras was finally leaving, and a new attorney general was taking over. The Guatemalans gathered outside the office had waited for this moment. What they had not anticipated was how long Porras’s departure would take, and how few people would come out to celebrate it. Thousands had massed in the same street just a few years before. When I met Arévalo a few days later, he justified the delay by explaining that his government had arrived “with an enormous level of public legitimacy, but without control of the Congress, and with the justice system positioned against us.” Legally, he had no authority to simply eject the attorney general. He sent a bill to Congress to grant him that power, but the opposition blocked it. “If, in that scenario, I make a political miscalculation, the result isn’t that I go with a hundred people to pull Consuelo Porras out of that building and that this is sustainable and produces results,” he said. It was that “I go to prison or into exile, and someone else comes in, one of them, to take power.” L ike much else in Guatemala , the colossal, mint-green presidential palace where Arévalo sat down with me is a holdover from a bygone era of authoritarianism. It was built by Guatemala’s Hitler-admiring, yet U.S.-backed dictator, Jorge Ubico, who rose to power in 1931 and was forced to resign amid mass protests in 1944. Arévalo, before winning the presidency, was best known as the son of the man who succeeded Ubico, in Guatemala’s first truly free elections. Juan José Arévalo, an educator and a social democrat, returned to Guatemala from exile in 1944 to run for president against the ex-dictator’s favored candidate. As his son would later, he won by a landslide, and Guatemala’s “democratic spring” began, a time of expanded rights and education. But after his freely and fairly elected successor, Jacobo Arbenz, went further, carrying out a land reform that threatened the interests of wealthy families and the powerful U.S.-based United Fruit Company, the United States organized a coup that put the military in power in 1954. Nine years later, a guerrilla leader asked Arévalo to help spearhead armed resistance to the regime, and the former president refused, saying that confronting the military head-on would turn Guatemala “into a lake of blood.” He was right. In the name of crushing the greatly outnumbered guerrillas, the military and its allies killed or disappeared more than 100,000 Guatemalans over the next three decades. It massacred leftists, labor leaders, and residents of more than 400 Maya villages suspected of supporting insurgents. Guatemalan courts eventually deemed the latter crime a genocide. Bernardo Arévalo, born in exile in Uruguay, returned with his family in the middle of the dictatorship period, and he began a career as a diplomat at its tail end, as the country formally returned to elections and civilian rule in 1985. He later left the diplomatic service, earned a Ph.D., and worked in international peace-building. The wood-paneled presidential office where we met was decorated only with two portraits: his father’s, in black-and-white, and his own, beside it, in color. Arévalo’s demeanor was professorial. “We are in a process of recovery,” he said. “Democracy doesn’t develop in a linear, unidirectional way; it has leaps and twists, not only here, but everywhere in the world.” For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Guatemala had been twisting its way toward democracy, but corruption networks and drug traffickers had insinuated themselves into the country’s institutions. “Part of what we set out to do is to recognize the serious damage this had caused the country—this corrosion, this penetration of political-criminal networks” that served no “ideological interest,” Arévalo said, but rather “the highest bidder: whoever could pay for impunity.” Dislodging these forces from the machinery of the state has been neither swift nor straightforward, and even those most anxious for change are hard-pressed to offer practical solutions. The president told me that some supporters had asked him to use the military to remove Porras. He found the suggestion unsettling: “Are you really asking us to go back to the years of military dictatorships of the 1970s, when armies were the only solution?” [ Read: A new history of the Western Hemisphere ] I asked Arévalo about the Indigenous protest leaders, Luis Pacheco and Hector Chaclán, who had then been imprisoned for more than a year while under investigation on terrorism charges. “I would like the people who say ‘But the government could have done something else’ to tell me what,” Arévalo replied, exasperated. “What they’re venting is the frustration we all feel.” He assured me that the pact of the corrupt was weakening incrementally as its networks lost access to the state: first the executive branch, then the public-works contracting system, now the prosecutor’s office. “Without tools, they aren’t powerful. And our task is to keep removing those tools from them.” Arévalo can point to some successes. Young lawyers have worked to clean up corruption in the judicial selection process. Appointed in March, the new bench of the Constitutional Court, which rules on the constitutionality of laws and policies, is more favorable to reformers than the one it replaced, as is the new electoral tribunal, which oversees elections. I spoke with the new attorney general a few days after he assumed his post: He was so busy firing Porras’s apparatchiks and preparing for the institution to resume serious criminal investigations that he was sleeping only four or five hours a night. An anti-corruption commission that Arévalo formed early on has already filed more than 200 criminal complaints against former officials. Arévalo was tasked with not only freeing a state captured by kleptocrats, but also strengthening one that was fundamentally weak. The bureaucracy he inherited had little capacity to provide public services, reduce poverty, or fight organized crime. In this, too, his administration has made some progress. It has hired more than 15,000 new teachers, and built or refurbished more than 150 rural-health clinics (his predecessor built just six in four years, Arévalo said). The government has also replaced dirt floors with cement in more than 75,000 households in the country’s poorest rural municipalities, and has distributed water filters and cleaner-burning stoves. Still, much else that Guatemalans had hoped for has failed to materialize. Congress, which remains dominated by the old-guard pact forces, has blocked or stalled bills aimed at curbing corruption—for example, bills to modernize public-works contracting, require shell companies to disclose who owns them, and protect whistleblowers. Partly because the contracting system remains dysfunctional, the government has made little visible progress toward repairing the country’s crumbling highways. And, unwilling to buy votes in Congress outright, as his predecessors did, Arévalo has resorted to pork-barrel spending and raising congressional salaries to win legislative support. Such tactics are deeply unpopular with the public. Another limiting factor has been the Trump administration. Although Arévalo’s cooperation on crime and drugs has kept the relationship cordial, his opponents have courted President Trump to try to tip the scales against reformers. In April, the U.S. ambassador to Guatemala personally called reluctant Guatemalan lawmakers to pressure them to approve a Constitutional Court judge favored by pact elites and conservatives, a top lawmaker, Luis Aguirre, told me. This tied the court between reformers and their opponents, leaving Arévalo without a reliable majority. T he young reformers who campaigned with Arévalo knew that he would face constraints, but some wish that he had more often tested those limits. Samuel Pérez, 34, is a member of Congress; he was also the head of the Seed Movement bloc in Congress before it was dissolved. I went to see him in a building plastered with missing-persons flyers for those who were disappeared during the military dictatorship decades ago. The flyers are a common sight in Guatemala City, posted and reposted by the victims’ families. Pérez told me that Arévalo was elected not only “to overthrow the regime, but also to construct something new, and that isn’t happening.” Now Pérez was creating a party, called Raíces, to which most of the lawmakers formerly associated with the Seed Movement had defected. They would still support Arévalo, but they would advocate for a more confrontational approach. “The president interprets power and good government as doing things a little better and a little more than what already existed. For me, no. You don’t use power to administrate what’s already there, but to transform what isn’t working,” Pérez explained. I’d last seen Pérez during Arévalo’s presidential campaign in 2023. He’d told me then that if the Seed Movement won, the government’s greatest difficulty would be managing popular expectations. But he hadn’t predicted that he himself would be among the disappointed. Arévalo should have rallied the public to pressure Congress to pass the law removing Porras, Pérez said. He should have conceded less to business elites, and done more to free Pacheco and Chaclán. Pérez was particularly upset that the police had come to arrest the two men in a white van with tinted windows—a symbol of the dictatorship, which used such vehicles to disappear its victims—and that the government had not stopped this. Several young Guatemalans in the reform movement suggested to me that the political caution of their parents’ generation was a product of the fear instilled in them during the years of military rule and internal armed conflict. Some speculated that Arévalo’s aversion to escalation emanates from that experience, too, given his youth in exile and the persecution of many of his father’s supporters in the years after the 1954 coup. “I think he is a son of his circumstances,” said Andrea Reyes, a young lawmaker helping Raíces organize. Arévalo readily locates his most formative influences in that era—as a source not of fear, but of strengthened conviction. He spoke to me of his father’s refusal to abandon democratic principles: “Even when the world began to change around him, he kept his convictions, which today we see were the correct convictions, after all, 80 years later.” Arévalo, too, has found his convictions under pressure—not only from former allies who worry that his reforms have gone too slowly, but also from constituents and conservative politicians who want a government that will ignore constitutional limits in cracking down on crime. In this they compare him unfavorably with the autocrat next door: Many Guatemalans who live in daily fear of extortion and kidnapping see gangs, not illiberal state capture, as the biggest threat to their basic freedoms, and they see President Nayib Bukele’s El Salvador as a beacon of safety. [ Read: El Salvador’s exceptional prison state ] Bukele, first elected in 2019, took an almost opposite approach from Arévalo’s to governing. He purged institutions of his political rivals, packed them with loyalists, and then cut secret deals with gang leaders before cracking down on their followers. His mass roundups virtually eliminated violent crime in his country, by jailing more than 90,000 people suspected of gang ties, many without due process. Arévalo is unwilling to pursue such methods. He has, however, seized record quantities of cocaine, extradited crime bosses, hired thousands of new police officers, and begun building the country’s first new maximum-security prison in 40 years. But murder and extortion rates have proved stubborn, and many are now demanding more-radical methods. “Guatemalans are searching for their Bukele,” said Alvaro Arzú Escobar, a conservative lawmaker sanctioned by the Biden administration for allegedly trying to undermine Arévalo’s inauguration. Arévalo “isn’t radical in his ideas or his actions,” Arzú told me. But, he added, “the country’s biggest problem right now is a lack of authority. As president, he doesn’t exercise the power he holds. There is a lot of rhetoric, but little action.” T he Mariscal Zavala military prison sits on a pine-covered ridge on the outskirts of Guatemala City. A former army base, it houses the state’s highest-profile prisoners. I went there to meet Pacheco and Chaclán, the Indigenous leaders who’d played such an instrumental role in safeguarding the 2023 presidential election. Both had been on the board of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán—one of the country’s oldest Indigenous self-governing bodies, in rural western Guatemala—when the attorney general’s office had moved to annul the vote. Pacheco and Chaclán canvassed rural villages on foot, helping gather some 50,000 signatures calling for Porras’s resignation. Later they helped organize protests in the capital. “The 48 Cantones is also a democracy, with elected leaders and term limits,” Chaclán told me. “For us, democracy is sacred, and although Guatemala often doesn’t reflect it much, we must respect it.” In April 2025, Porras ordered him and Pacheco into pretrial detention. After that, their court hearings were repeatedly delayed, seemingly intentionally, and when I met them in May, they had no idea when the next one would be. I asked them whether they believed Arévalo should have rallied protesters or found some other tool to remove Porras, and thus to free them. Pacheco responded, “I would have liked it at first, but later I realized it would have only changed the person, not the form of doing justice.” Chaclán added, “This is nothing simple, and surely he is doing what is best for the country. We have faith we have already passed the majority of our time here.” Chaclán was right. On August 5, a judge released Pacheco and Chaclán to house arrest, reuniting them with their families. Around the same time, the prison-like, black-steel fence was taken down from around the public prosecutor’s office. Guatemala’s next presidential election is just nine months away. Right-wing candidates are beginning to emerge, some imitating Bukele, and many sure to court the White House, in the hope that Trump will try to tip the scales. Arévalo’s and Pérez’s reformists claim that they will join forces behind a unity candidate, but such a figure has not yet surfaced. Democracy is twisting its way forward, in Arévalo’s words. No one thinks it is leaping. But the passage of time may provide a different perspective. On one of my last days in Guatemala City, I walked by a cathedral I had passed dozens of times before. I had never previously noticed the tiny engraved names of more than 13,000 victims of the internal armed conflict, so small as to be illegible from even a short distance, on its stone columns. For much of the 20th century, Guatemalans who advocated for self-government, equality before the law, and the welfare of the majority—that is, social democrats—knew that the state might try to kill them. Today, social democrats govern. Reformers may disagree as to whether Bernardo Arévalo made the most of the opportunity he was given. But that such an opportunity could ever arise is more than many members of his father’s generation likely thought possible. *Image Sources: Luis Soto / AP; Johan Ordonez / AFP / Getty; Arnulfo Franco / AFP / Getty.

items.title: 190 Days Without a Homicide
items.description: J enee Gragston dropped to the ground and held on to the grass as if it could save her life. She yelled to her family members to get down. She later told me that she didn’t know where the bullets were coming from, but she knew they were close. When the firing stopped, the cries began. She could hear her 4-year-old nephew howling: “Get it off me! Get it off me!” She wasn’t close enough to see what had happened, but it looked like he had blood on his chest. A teenage boy was lying near the child. The teenager “never screamed or anything,” she said. “I can still see all of it.” It was a Saturday afternoon, mid-August in Lexington, Kentucky. Hundreds of people had gathered in Charles Young Park to celebrate what’s called East End Day—a combination of family reunions, live music, and lots of food. I grew up going to festivals in that park, though I lived on the west side of town, in the Charlotte Court housing projects. Kentucky isn’t the most dangerous place in America, but it’s up there, with the 14th-highest rate of gun deaths. Twelve years ago, my uncle was murdered in Lexington. Three years ago, my sister’s husband was shot and killed there. I worry about my brother, who still lives there. He had gotten himself off the streets for a while, but is now back living in the city. Lexington had recently seen a hard-won drop in gun deaths—last year was the fourth straight year of declines in gun violence among young people. This spring and summer set a record of 190 straight days without a homicide. Then came the East End Day shooting, which killed that teenager, 16-year-old Di’Zhon Robertson, and wounded four others—including the 4-year-old, who was shot in the leg. The next weekend, another person was killed. The weekend after that, four separate shootings left two more dead. Gragston was selling Polish sausages in the park. She’d paid more than $300 for the grill, $300 for the sausages, more than $1,000 in fees, $75 for the booth. Business was good; some people returned for seconds. Her husband, her kids, and other family members had come to help her set up her tent. Her 4-year-old nephew was handing customers sodas and water bottles. On the basketball court nearby, Devine Carama was talking with a group of young people. Carama is the director of ONE Lexington, a city-funded program that tries to prevent gun violence by mentoring at-risk boys. He, too, threw himself down when he heard gunfire. “I almost got shot that day,” he told me. Two people near him were hit—a man and his girlfriend. Carama and others tried to bandage the man’s leg; he told me he could see a glimmer of bullet or bone through the blood. [ Sari Horwitz: The gun lobby’s most cynical move yet ] A day later, 18-year-old Jametrius Griffin turned himself in and was charged with murder. According to court testimony , Griffin’s younger brother had gotten into an argument; punches were thrown, and the younger brother fell or was pushed. When Griffin saw that, he yanked out a gun and started firing. For the past three years, Robertson had participated in ONE Lexington’s summer youth program, which offers workshops on building emotional and social skills, as well as college-campus visits. “He wasn’t a street kid,” Carama said. Griffin’s younger brother was in ONE Lexington, too—in its school mentoring program. The organization had also helped Griffin get a job at UPS. The group’s work seemed to be making a difference. And then a fight left one young man dead, one wounded, and one in prison. I n many ways, Lexington feels like a small town, where everyone knows everyone. I went to middle school with Griffin’s lawyer, Daniel Whitley, who has a big reputation locally for representing people accused of murder—and for winning their cases. The week after the shooting, I spoke with Whitley and with Griffin’s mother, Jay-Me Baxter, on a video call. “A bunch of bullshit” was how Baxter described the park shooting, “because everybody’s friends and everybody’s family.” She said her youngest son told her he had been bullied by Di’Zhon Robertson and others.
